labels.name: ggml
labels.description: changes relating to the ggml tensor library for machine learning

items.body:
## Overview

Follow-up to #28069, which added the simdgroup CONV_2D kernel for all Apple Silicon. While approving it, @ggerganov asked for an M5 Tensor API implementation: this PR adds it, and also speeds up the #28069 kernel on every chip.

On devices with the tensor API (M5), CONV_2D now runs as a matmul on the tensor cores, like `kernel_mul_mm`: the patches of 64 output positions are gathered into threadgroup memory and the kernel rows are read directly from device memory. M1 to M4 keep the simdgroup kernel of #28069.

Both kernels can now split long reductions. Convolutions with few output positions and thousands of reduction terms used to run a handful of threadgroups on an idle GPU. The partial sums go to a buffer after the output and are added in a fixed order, so the result stays deterministic. The patch gather walks 32-bit byte offsets instead of recomputing the indices for every value.

It also includes the nit I left on #28069: the simdgroup count was hardcoded to 4 in both the kernel and its pipeline, it now comes from a single `N_SG_CONV_2D` so the dispatch and the kernel cannot drift apart.

`test-backend-ops perf -o CONV_2D`, F16 kernel, M5 Max, us/run (the two 1D rows are audio decoder shapes added locally, they are not in the perf suite):

| input | kernel | master | this PR | speedup |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| [19,19,256,16] | [4,4,256,4096] | 19103 | 4004 | 4.77x |
| [1536,1536,32,1] | [3,3,32,64] | 12245 | 5199 | 2.36x |
| [16,16,128,8] | [3,3,128,512] | 333 | 100 | 3.34x |
| [58,58,32,1] | [3,3,32,64] | 39 | 15 | 2.57x |
| [224,224,1,8] | [2,2,1,8] | 112 | 89 | 1.25x |
| [2054,1,768,1] | [7,1,768,768] | 3168 | 546 | 5.80x |
| [33,1,1280,1] stride 2 | [3,1,1280,1280] | 664 | 34 | 19.79x |

The 22 cases of the perf suite (11 shapes, F16 and F32 kernels) all get faster, from 1.11x to 4.77x. With `GGML_METAL_TENSOR_DISABLE=1`, which runs the simdgroup kernel of M1 to M4, the split and the cheaper gather give 1.10x to 1.29x on long reductions and 10.7x on the narrow [33,1,1280,1] case.

## Overview

Fix a 32-bit integer overflow in the `mul_mv` destination offset calculation for large batched outputs.

When `im * args.ne0 * args.ne1` exceeds `INT32_MAX`, the offset can overflow, causing the affected destination slices to remain unwritten.

Promote the offset arithmetic to `uint64_t` before multiplication.

Fixes #30237.

Reproduced on Apple M5 with the Metal backend.

Before the fix:

```text
RESULT mv: FAIL (bad=2097152 of 2149580800)
```

After the fix:

```text
RESULT mv: OK (bad=0 of 2149580800)
```

## Overview

items.title: metal: align command buffer splits on fusion groups for stable output

labels.name: ggml
labels.description: changes relating to the ggml tensor library for machine learning

items.body:
## Overview

No change in speed or output quality, this is a developer fix:
With this PR, the greedy output on Metal no longer depends on the node count of the graph: two graphs that compute the same thing give the same tokens, as on CUDA. This makes bit-exact A/B comparisons on Metal reliable again (master vs a branch, a refactor before and after), for developers as well as for automated verification loops, instead of chasing a divergence that looks like a bug but is not one.

The cause: Metal encodes the first 10% of the graph nodes in a first command buffer, so the GPU starts while the rest is encoded, and splits the rest evenly between the extra command buffers. A fusion cannot span two command buffers, so when a boundary falls inside a fusable group, that group runs unfused and its rounding changes, and where the boundary falls depends on the node count.

This PR moves each boundary to the end of the fusable group it falls into, using the same ggml_metal_fusion_max() that the graph optimizer uses to pack these groups, so the encoders fuse the same nodes as with a single command buffer.

## Additional information

Found while comparing #31660 with master on GLM-5.3-Flash with MTP: with master's node count the boundary falls inside the MoE reduce of layer 4, while with the PR it does not, and the top-k selections of the model amplify that rounding difference into different accept rates. With this PR, master and #31660 give the exact same output on an M5 Max, same text and same drafts.

It changes neither speed nor quality: llama-bench on an M5 Max (GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-27B, pp512 and tg128) stays within 1%, and the fused and unfused paths are both correct, only their rounding differs. test-backend-ops on the fused ops, test-llama-archs and test-llama-context pass on Metal.

items.title: metal : guard flash-attn vec output scratch zeroing

labels.name: ggml
labels.description: changes relating to the ggml tensor library for machine learning

items.body:
## Overview

In `kernel_flash_attn_ext_vec`, `so4` points to a threadgroup scratch buffer associated with each SIMD group. Before the zero-initialization loop, this pointer is offset based on the lane index; however, all 32 lanes execute the loop. When `DK = DV = 64`, `Q = 1`, and `NE = 4`, a given lane might access the lement at index 39, even though the SIMD group to which it belongs only encompasses 32 elements within that buffer.

By adding the condition `(DV4/NL % NW == 0) || tiisg < NL` to constrain the zero-initialization loop, we ensure consistency with the condition used during subsequent updates to `so4`.

On an M2 Mac running macOS 27.2, metal shader validation of a build based on `28b812d6c` revealed such out-of-bounds write operations. With a head size of 64, applying this patch reduced the number of reported out-of-bounds accesses from 109 to 0.

## Overview

The Metal TOPK_MOE fusion only covered plain-softmax routing with a lower-clamp norm, so DeepSeek-V4/V4.1 layers never fused. This PR adds three things:

- New fusion chains anchored at the sigmoid node (UNARY+ADD+ARGSORT+GET_ROWS plus optional norm/scale) so sigmoid-gated routing (GLM, DeepSeek-V2/V3.2, ...) fuses on Metal. As with sqrt(softplus), the kernel ranks selection-biased keys while the gathered routing weights and their norm stay unbiased.

labels.description: A maintainer can use this label to indicate that they consider the changes final and ready to merge.

items.body:
## Overview

On iOS 27, after a model is freed, `phys_footprint` still includes the memory that ggml has just freed. Mac Catalyst apps on macOS 27.0.1 behave the same way. `os_proc_available_memory()` follows `phys_footprint`, so an app that checks the available memory before it loads the next model sees less than it really has.

That's because `ggml_aligned_malloc` and the Metal host buffers use `posix_memalign` and `free` on every Apple platform except macOS. On iOS 27 and macOS 27.0.1, libmalloc keeps large freed blocks in the process footprint and gives the pages back later. It's not a leak, since the kernel takes the pages back before the process reaches its memory limit.

On macOS these buffers already use `vm_allocate` and `vm_deallocate` (#7078, #9875), and `vm_deallocate` gives the pages back right away. This PR uses them on all Apple platforms. In `ggml.c` the 2 `TARGET_OS_OSX` checks become `defined(__APPLE__)`. `ggml-metal-device.m` is only built for Apple platforms, so its `posix_memalign` fallback is removed. This covers iOS, the iOS simulator, Mac Catalyst, tvOS, visionOS and watchOS.

I added `test-host-buffer-release`, which runs by default on Apple platforms. For both the CPU buffer type and `MTL0`, it allocates a 256 MiB buffer and frees it. Right after the free, it checks that `phys_footprint` dropped by more than 75% of the buffer size.

Results from a Mac Catalyst build on an M3 Ultra with macOS 27.0.1, showing `phys_footprint` before -> after the free:

| | CPU buffer | MTL0 buffer | test |
|---|---|---|---|
| master | 260.5 -> 260.5 MiB | 536.2 -> 552.2 MiB | fails |
| this PR | 260.5 -> 4.4 MiB | 645.6 -> 389.5 MiB | passes |

For macOS builds the change compiles to the same code as before. The test passes on macOS with and without Metal, and in the Mac Catalyst build. iOS, tvOS and visionOS build with the `build-apple.yml` commands (iOS and tvOS with deployment target 15.0, the lowest Xcode 27 accepts), and no warning points at the changed lines. No CI job builds watchOS, and `ggml-base` does not build for it on master either (`ggml-backend.cpp` fails in the SDK headers), but `ggml.c` compiles for arm64 and arm64_32 with the same warnings as on master. I haven't run the test on tvOS, visionOS or watchOS.

## Additional information

Ref #30556

#31438 moves the loader's staging buffer to the CPU buffer type. On iOS, that change only helps together with this PR.

## Overview

Port `GGML_OP_TOP_K_MASK` from the CUDA backend (#30640) to the Metal backend. items.body:
CPY fails at random on SYCL for f16/bf16 to q2_0, q4_0 and q5_0. Random because the test data is random.

The device rounds three things differently from the CPU, by one ulp each: the reciprocal of 1.0f/d, the fused multiply and add in x*id + 8.5f (q4_0) and + 16.5f (q5_0), and the (int)(x + 0.5f) round in q2_0. f16/bf16 inputs sit on exact .5 ties, so one ulp flips the quantised value.

The fix is in ggml/src/ggml-sycl/cpy.hpp: correctly rounded division, round half away from zero by truncation, and a no-op fmin so the multiply and add don't fuse. Only the f32 to qX_0 block functions change.

From review: ggml/src/ggml-metal/kernels/quantize.h gets the `#pragma METAL fp math_mode(safe)` that quantize_q2_0 was missing (the other quantizers already have it).

100 runs of test-backend-ops -o CPY: 70/100 fail on master, 0/100 with the fix. Runs with any failure go from 78 to 30, the rest are q4_1, q8_0 and q5_1, which also fail on master and aren't touched here.

## Overview

This implementation uses contiguous slices instead of interleaved, considering tied numbers in column order: block by block, by warp, then by step and by lane. Earliest tie wins. 

Order for values above the threshold isn't deterministic just as before. So we make best effort to not to pay for correctness with speed.

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

## Additional information

| TOP_K variant | Mean KLD | Same top p |
| --- | --- | --- |
| master | 0.0011 | 99.48% | 
| warp-alignas | 0.000000 | 100.000% | 

We have a tie when there are N biggest numbers such as N>k and some smallest largest numbers are equal (there are more numbers equal v than there are slots left for them). In the prior implementation the choice of a position of the smallest largest number depended on the thread timing. This caused a non-deterministic KLD (from 0.0004 to 0.011 between runs).

- As caught in the QSA indexer only for MoE fusions: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31009#pullrequestreview-5655765863

- Although the test identified other backends as broken, I did not include any changes to them as this implementation is not finialized. And besides they could use their own PRs.

- With CCCL 3.4.3 or newer, one or two rows still go through DeviceTopK (single token decode for the indexer), so ties there stay nondeterministic: the test skips this combination.

I tried a handful of ways to untangle this, and the current variant is the fastest:

| 200000x16 k=400 | 45.61 | 37.83 | 0.83 |
| **geomean** | | | **0.89** |

Benchmarks for other variants:

| case | master | interleaved | tile | composite | warp |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4096x16 k=16 | 29.18 | 29.45 | 28.04 | 21.32 | 28.04 |
| 32768x16 k=16 | 27.03 | 26.42 | 25.87 | 27.24 | 25.80 |
| 32768x16 k=2048 | 35.47 | 30.85 | 29.56 | 25.11 | 29.43 |
| 65000x16 k=1 | 35.44 | 36.10 | 34.67 | 31.03 | 34.59 |

| 65000x16 k=400 | 42.25 | 38.16 | 36.53 | 34.27 | 36.48 |
| 131072x32 k=2048 | 61.65 | 53.40 | 46.91 | 47.30 | 46.55 |
| 200000x16 k=1 | 44.48 | 45.80 | 38.66 | 50.82 | 36.86 |
| 200000x16 k=16 | 48.41 | 48.92 | 42.28 | 43.97 | 40.14 |

| **geomean / master** | 1.00 | 0.97 | 0.89 | 0.87 | 0.87 |

```
test-backend-ops perf -o TOP_K -b CUDA0 -p 'ne=\[(131072,32|4096,16|200000,1|1000,1|32768,16|8192,1|200000,16|65000,16),1,1\],k=(1|16|400|2048),'
```

| variant | fix | 
|---|---|
| interleaved | the threads keep master's strided reads, and a block-wide prefix sum gives the ties a fixed order (by block, then thread, then column), which is deterministic but not lowest-index | 
| tile | each block reads a contiguous range of columns, and a block-wide prefix sum ranks the ties in column order, so the lowest columns win | 
| composite | the key is a 64-bit pair of the value and the column, so no two keys are equal and the radix select has no ties | 
| warp | each warp reads a contiguous part of the block range, and a warp ballot ranks the ties in column order, so the lowest columns win with one `__syncthreads` per block |
| warp-aggr | as warp, but one atomic per warp for the values above the threshold, and no `alignas(128)` on the row state |

- SGLang simply uses a less performant process when asked for deterministic outputs

- vLLM is deterministic only for small tie groups
- CUB DeviceTopK only implements "not deterministic" so far, both CCCL 3.4 and 3.5.

## Overview

On Metal, matmuls with batch > 8 use `mul_mm` only when K >= 64. Below that, `mul_mv` is used: `_short` for K < 32, and the generic kernel for K >= 32. The generic kernel is built for long rows, so at K = 32–63 its per-row reduction and dispatch overhead dominate. At n = 512, K = 32 runs 32x slower than K = 64, despite half the math.

LoRA matrices have K = rank, so rank 32–63 adapters hit this. On master, an r32 or r48 adapter roughly halves prefill speed; r16 and r64 don't (about 16% of popular LoRA adapters on Hugging Face are r32, also my research team choose r32 for good result enough).

This change sends 32 <= K < 64 to `mul_mm`, which already supports it: it steps K by 32 and zero-pads the tail.
- K < 32 is unchanged; `mul_mm` is slower there at small batch.

All numbers are from an Apple M4 (10-core GPU), macOS 27.0.1.

## Overview

Add a generic batched tensor copy API to ggml that supersedes the existing `_2d` API and supports arbitrary batches of tensors.

The API uses parallel arrays instead of structs:

- `ggml_backend_tensor_set_n`
- `ggml_backend_tensor_get_n`
- `ggml_backend_tensor_copy_n`

A generic fallback is provided: if the backend implements `_n`, it is used; otherwise regular 2D-shaped batches reuse the `_2d` path, and remaining batches are decomposed into per-tensor `set`/`get`/`copy` calls.

When a batch spans multiple backend buffer types, the tensors are grouped by buffer type and each group is processed through the same `_n` fallback chain. This lets mixed-buffer batches still benefit from backend-specific batching.

The internal buffer interface takes arrays of data pointers (`const void * const *` / `void * const *`) so backends can batch copies from arbitrary host buffers without assuming contiguity. The public API keeps `data + data_offsets` for ergonomics.

The Metal and CUDA backends implement the buffer-level `_n` hooks:

- `set_tensor_n`
- `get_tensor_n`
- `cpy_tensor_n`

`cpy_tensor_n` is all-or-nothing: if it returns `false`, no copies have been performed and the caller falls back to per-tensor copies.

All other backend buffer interfaces explicitly set these hooks to `NULL` and rely on the generic fallback.

`llama_io_write_host`, `llama_io_read_host`, `llama_io_write_device`, and `llama_io_read_device` now use the batched API for context save/load.

## Additional information

Dedicated backend-enumerating test added in `tests/test-backend-tensor.cpp`, covering irregular batches, regular 2D-shaped batches, zero-size entries, and batches that span multiple buffer types.

- Implement `_n` in all backends

## Overview

The fused `MOE_REDUCE` Metal kernel (`kernel_moe_reduce_f32`) computes `dst = Σ experts[e]·weights[e]` in a single dispatch, reading `experts` and `weights` while writing `dst`. The graph allocator computes tensor liveness on the unfused graph, where the inputs are fully consumed by earlier nodes of the fused group, so it can legally recycle the input memory as `dst` — in the fused kernel that becomes a threadgroup-vs-threadgroup race inside a single dispatch, producing rare non-deterministic wrong results.

Fix: reject the fusion at encode time when `dst` overlaps either input, using the existing `ggml_metal_fusion_overlap` helper — the same guard pattern as the `MUL_MAT_ADD` fusion. The unfused MUL + ADD path is always correct.

## Overview

ggml_tri kept the selected elements by scaling them with the 0/1 comparison:

    dst_row[i0] = static_cast<T>(_ggml_vec_tri_cmp<ttype>(i0, i1)) * src_row[i0];

items.body:
## Overview

- Fixes Metal `MUL_MAT_ID` for duplicate ids (the new tests from #29998): the old `kernel_mul_mm_id_map0` assumed at most one match per token and a fixed capacity of `ne21` entries per expert, which produced wrong or dropped output rows and could overflow into the slice of the next expert.
- The prepass (`kernel_mul_mm_id_map0`) builds a compact per-expert list of `(token, slot)` entries: pass 1 counts the entries of every expert, thread 0 computes the offsets of the expert slices and emits a row map - the total tile count plus one `(expert, first entry, valid rows)` descriptor per 32-entry tile that has work - and pass 2 fills the slices with one unconditional store per token (stores from divergent lanes are very slow; the dummy value of the tokens without a match lands on a padding slot that is never read), with duplicates handled by a rare branch.
- Following the vulkan approach from #29998, `kernel_mul_mm_id` is launched with a static upper bound on the tiles (`min(n_rows, ceil(n_rows/32) + min(n_experts, n_rows) - 1)`), reads its descriptor and processes a single tile - the tail early exits. This replaces the previous experts x ne21 grid (mostly threadgroups that launched only to exit, ~94% on typical shapes) and removes the need for any per-expert loop, so duplicate ids are covered implicitly and the kernel's register pressure is back to the plain `mul_mat_id` level.
- The ids buffer is sized `ne20*ne21 + ne02` (entries + one padding slot per expert); `ne02` is passed to `kernel_mul_mm_id_map0` as a function constant and its id loops use `FOR_UNROLL`.
- Also includes the dispatch limits / pipeline-name fix from the branch head (`ne02 <= 1024` guard in `ggml_metal_op_mul_mat_id_use_mm`, `_ne20` pipeline name suffix).

items.body:
Fixes #30064.

## Overview

`ggml_metal_op_mul_mat_mma` picks the residual of a fused `MUL_MAT+ADD` as "the ADD operand whose op is not `MUL_MAT`":

```cpp
res = dst->src[0]->op == GGML_OP_MUL_MAT ? dst->src[1] : dst->src[0];
```

When **both** ADD operands are mat-mul outputs (`x = W1 @ u + W2 @ v`) that test is true for both, so `res` resolves to the fused mat-mul's *own* output — a buffer
nothing ever writes — and the MMA store adds whatever it holds. The fusion check (`ggml_metal_mul_mat_add_operand`) already selects the operand by identity; this
makes the encoder do the same.

Clef decision models hit this in the head (`src/models/clef.cpp`): `options = proj_option_context @ opt_ctx + proj_option_lexical @ lexical`, 9 option rows. Symptoms
match #30064 exactly:

| | billing | technical |
|---|---|---|
| Metal, default | 0.284 | 0.431 |
| Metal, `GGML_METAL_GRAPH_OPTIMIZE_DISABLE=1` | 0.462 | 0.254 |
| Metal, `GGML_METAL_FUSION_DISABLE=1` | **0.977** | 0.009 |
| Metal, only the `MUL_MAT+ADD` fusion row removed | **0.977** | 0.008 |
| CPU | **0.977** | 0.009 |
| Metal, this patch | **0.977** | 0.008 |

(`Cloudflare_clef-flash-Q8_0`, the model card's double-charge request, M1 Max.) Deterministic per memory layout, which is why the value shifts with graph optimize
off. Not a quantization issue — the same Q8_0 file is right on the CPU backend — so the "keep `decision.*` at BF16" workaround in the issue is working around this
bug.

## Test

New `MUL_MAT_ADD` mode `mm2+mm` in `test-backend-ops`: the residual is a second mat-mul of the same shape. On Metal at `48499d2e1` it fails **27 of 28** cases before

## Overview

Speculative decoding verifies a few draft tokens per step, and batched decoding runs one row per sequence, so the model runs mat-muls with 2..16 src1 rows. On Apple GPUs without the tensor API (M1 to M4), Metal runs these with the mat-vec kernels, whose time grows with each row. On an M3 Ultra, DFlash2 decoding of Qwen3.8-27B is therefore slower than serial decoding on master.

This PR adds:

- Mat-mul kernels for 2..16 src1 rows on 8x8 simdgroup matrices. Each weight is dequantized once for all rows, and the simdgroups of a threadgroup split K. Q4_0, Q8_0 and Q5_K have their own kernels. F32, F16, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q4_K and Q6_K use a generic path over the existing 16-weight dequantizers. Q4_0 at 2 rows uses a 2-row variant of the mat-vec kernel.
- The kernels fill simdgroup matrices per lane, so they run only on MTLGPUFamilyApple7+ without the tensor API. They start at the row count where they beat the mat-vec kernels on an M3 Ultra: 6 for F32, 3 for F16, Q4_K, Q5_0 and Q5_1, and 2 for the other types.
- A fusion table entry: MUL_MAT + ADD writes the residual sum from the MMA store.
- CONCAT splits long rows across threadgroups when there are few rows.

## Additional information

Changes to the fusion and reorder code:

- The fusion checks, `ggml_metal_fusion_next`, `ggml_metal_fusion_max` and `ggml_graph_optimize` take the device props, so the reorder packs MUL_MAT + ADD only on devices that fuse it. The pack does not depend on the src1 row count, so graphs of different batch sizes get the same node order (no reallocation with `GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC`).
- The alloc-deps pass also matches the new MUL_MAT + ADD pattern, so on every Metal device the mat-mul inputs stay alive until the ADD.

items.title: qwen4exp : halve the indexer score memory

labels.name: Vulkan

labels.name: ggml
labels.description: changes relating to the ggml tensor library for machine learning

items.body:
## Overview

The qwen4exp indexer was wasting memory: it computed the scores of all its heads at once, then made a full copy of them for the relu, before summing everything into a single score. At 131k context with -b 4096 that is about 4 GB of intermediates to produce a 0.5 GB result, and the largest buffers of the whole graph.

It now scores one head at a time, with the relu done in place, and adds each head into the score as it goes. Same computation, same top-k selection, half the compute buffer.

Confirmed by @LucaAmigoni on the full model with two GPUs: -b 4096 with the default -np loads again without OOM, as before #29751.

CUDA compute buffer, micro qwen4exp with the real QSA config (4 indexer heads, top_k 2048, kpool 4):
- c 131072, ub 2048: 3.0 GiB -> 1.5 GiB
- c 131072, ub 4096: 6.1 GiB -> 3.0 GiB
- c 262144, ub 4096: 11.7 GiB -> 5.6 GiB

The scores only differ by fp32 rounding from the matmul reduction order, logits are bit-exact, test-llama-archs passes, and pp/tg speed is unchanged.

The rest of the reserve is the dense [n_kv, n_tokens] selection mask from the TODO in build_qsa_sel: it already reuses one buffer, so going below it needs flash_attn_ext to take the selected cell indices instead of a mask.

## Overview

During multi-seq inference, unified kv-cache pays a big penalty due to having to filter out other sequence tokens from the mask. Queries shared the kv rows and their mask + a new data struct `kv_rows` enables an indirect look-up for a compact representation of the required tokens per seq.

items.title: metal : fix threadgroup memory overflow in quantized flash attention

labels.name: ggml
labels.description: changes relating to the ggml tensor library for machine learning

items.body:
## Overview

Overflow happens when quantized KV at head sizes 512/512 or 576/512 with batches of 20-31 tokens needs more than 32 KiB of threadgroup memory. The fix dequantizes KV to F16 before running the non-vec kernel while preserving vec dispatch. See example below:

```
// Q8_0 KV, DK/DV = 576/512, ne01 = 24
// nqptg = 8, ncpsg = 64, nsg = 8

BEFORE
  use_vec:
    (24 < 20) && (576 % 32 == 0)
    -> false

  use_kv_f16 early-return guard:
    24 < 32
    -> true -> returns false

  is_q = 1
  smem = (8*(576 + 1024 + 256) + 4096)*2
       = 37888 > 32768
  Metal validation aborts.

AFTER
  use_kv_f16 early-return guard:
    (24 < 32) && (576 < 512 || use_vec)
    -> true && (false || false)
    -> false -> guard not taken

  type switch:
    Q8_0 -> returns true

  is_q = 0
  smem = (8*(576 + 1024 + 256))*2
       = 29696 <= 32768
```

Adds regression cases for both shapes: each fails without the fix and passes with Metal validation enabled; the full FA suite passes 4956/4956.

## Additional information

Found while working on #28439, The regression tests require MTL_DEBUG_LAYER=1 MTL_DEBUG_LAYER_ERROR_MODE=assert; without validation, both cases pass even without the fix.

labels.name: ggml
labels.description: changes relating to the ggml tensor library for machine learning

items.body:
## Overview

The Metal FWHT covers block widths 64 to 512. It runs one row per simdgroup and keeps
`N/32` values per lane, so wider blocks need more registers per lane than that layout
allows.

`kernel_fwht_tg` runs one row per threadgroup with 256 threads, so each thread keeps
`N/256` values instead. Butterflies below the simdgroup width still shuffle, those up to
the threadgroup width go through threadgroup memory, and the rest stay in registers. The
butterfly and sign convention match the existing kernel.

Widths 64 to 512 keep the simdgroup kernel and are untouched. 1024 through 8192 use the
new one, for both F32 and F16 sources.

## Additional information

Stacked on #29094, which adds the F16 source type. The last commit is the one to review here.

8192 allocates 32 KB of threadgroup memory, which is the limit on the devices I can test.
`ggml_metal_fwht_supported_size` stops there for that reason, and anything wider keeps the
existing behaviour of falling back to the generic matmul path.

Tested on an M5 Pro with `test-backend-ops`:
- `MUL_MAT_HADAMARD` 26/26, including the new 1024/2048/4096/8192 cases in F32 and F16
- `MUL_MAT` 1265/1265, no regressions

The previous "too big" test case moved from 1024 to 16384, since 1024 is now covered.

None of this says the pooled rows pick faster kernels. In-sample they are 98.5% of per-device tuning at the attention level — marginally slower — which end to end is below what this test can resolve.

This change modifies the `kernel_mul_mm` implementation in `ggml/src/ggml-metal/kernels/mul_mm.metal` for the `GGML_METAL_HAS_TENSOR == true` path. Instead of using the `slice` method, it explicitly computes the address of each slice and constructs the tensor directly from the computed address. Related issue: #27784 After this change, the issue is no longer reproducible. ```bash sending long embedding request... long: output_size=1024 invalid_values=0 * Terminal will be reused by tasks, press any key to close it. * Executing task: python3 scripts/issue27784_probe.py sending short embedding request... short: output_size=1024 invalid_values=0 * Terminal will be reused by tasks, press any key to close it. ``` ## Additional information ### Environment Hardware: Apple MacBook Air 13 inch M5 16G macOS: 26.6.2 (25G83) Metal compiler: Apple metal version 32023.883 (metalfe-32023.883), Target: air64-apple-darwin25.6.0, Thread model: posix ### Experiment Design Each case runs the same matrix multiplication with a K dimension of `16`, producing a cooperative tensor `cT`. ## Overview

On macOS, any depthwise 1D convolution over bf16 weights aborts with:

"kernel not found in any metal library: kernel_mul_mv_f32_bf16_short"

ggml_conv_1d_dw builds its im2col as f32 when the kernel is bf16, then calls mul_mat(im2col, kernel), which puts f32 in src0 and bf16 in src1. That combination is never instantiated: the library has f32_f32, f16_f32, f16_f16, bf16_f32 and bf16_bf16, but not f32_bf16. Other convolution paths do not hit it because conv_2d keeps its im2col in f16 whatever the kernel type.

## Additional information

I paid attention to the guard because I have had that exact point raised on a previous PR, the bf16 kernels must stay behind GGML_METAL_HAS_BF16. The three variants are added next to their bf16 neighbours, inside the existing `#if defined(GGML_METAL_HAS_BF16)` block. That macro is injected at library compile time only when the device reports bf16 support, so devices without it are unaffected.

items.title: metal : skip the empty half of the mul_mm_id token tile, load iq2/iq3 codebooks as uint32

labels.name: ggml
labels.description: changes relating to the ggml tensor library for machine learning

items.body:
## Overview

`kernel_mul_mm_id` works on 32 routed token rows at a time. An expert often receives fewer than 32 rows, but the unused rows are still multiplied and discarded.

This splits the token tile into two `NR1H = 16` halves and skips the upper half when `nr1 <= NR1H`.

On the tensor-ops path, each half gets its own `matmul2d` call. On the simdgroup path, the two simdgroups responsible for rows 16..31 are disabled through `sg_active` when the upper half is not needed.

`nr1` is the number of rows remaining in the current tile. An expert with 33 routed rows therefore gets one full tile and a 1-row tail, and the tail skips its upper half.

The `tB` extents are also corrected for the split tile. They were `(NR1, NK)` for a `[NR1][NK]` row-major tile, which was harmless while both dimensions were 32.

For reference, mean rows per expert are:

```text
ubatch * n_expert_used / n_expert
```

A 256-expert top-8 model therefore averages 8 rows per expert at `-ub 256` and 16 at `-ub 512`.

`mul_mm_id` is used from 32 tokens up. Below that, MoE uses `mul_mv_id`, so this kernel is not reached.

The IQ codebook and padding-staging changes from the first revision have been removed. This PR now contains only the tile split, the `tB` extent fix, and the related tests/benchmark hook.


## Performance

Apple M5, against master `5a4d0feca`. Four paired runs per case. Negative is faster.

### Tensor ops

```sh
./build/bin/test-backend-ops perf -o MUL_MAT_ID -b MTL0 \
  -p "type_a=(q4_0|q4_K|iq2_xs|iq2_s|iq3_xxs),.*,n=(64|128|256|512|1024|2048),"
```

| n | q4_0 | q4_K | iq2_xs | iq2_s | iq3_xxs |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 | -4.5% | -11.4% | -18.1% | -16.5% | -15.2% |
| 128 | -5.4% | -8.7% | -13.7% | -13.5% | -11.3% |
| 256 | -4.0% | -3.8% | -7.6% | -6.9% | -5.8% |
| 512 | -3.0% | -0.8% | -4.4% | -4.6% | -3.4% |
| 1024 | -3.4% | -2.0% | -3.9% | -4.0% | -1.8% |
| 2048 | +0.2% | +1.2% | +0.3% | -0.7% | +0.6% |

The largest regression is +1.2% for `q4_K` at `n = 2048`. At smaller batch sizes, where experts receive fewer rows, the gain is larger.

`iq2_s`, `iq3_xxs`, and `n > 512` are not in the upstream perf set. I added them locally for these measurements; the test change is not part of this PR.

<details>
<summary>Measurement-only test-backend-ops change</summary>

```diff
@@ static std::vector<std::unique_ptr<test_case>> make_test_cases_perf() {
     // qwen3-30b-a3b
-    for (int bs : {1, 4, 8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512}) {
-        for (ggml_type type_a : {GGML_TYPE_F32, GGML_TYPE_F16, GGML_TYPE_Q4_0, GGML_TYPE_Q8_0, GGML_TYPE_Q4_K, GGML_TYPE_Q6_K, GGML_TYPE_IQ2_XS}) {
+    for (int bs : {1, 4, 8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048}) {
+        for (ggml_type type_a : {GGML_TYPE_F32, GGML_TYPE_F16, GGML_TYPE_Q4_0, GGML_TYPE_Q8_0, GGML_TYPE_Q4_K, GGML_TYPE_Q6_K, GGML_TYPE_IQ2_XS, GGML_TYPE_IQ2_S, GGML_TYPE_IQ3_XXS}) {
             for (ggml_type type_b : {GGML_TYPE_F32}) {
                 test_cases.emplace_back(new test_mul_mat_id(type_a, type_b, 128, 8, false, 768, bs, 2048));
```

The same change was made to the `32, 4, false, 1792` loop below it.

</details>

### Simdgroup path

```sh
GGML_METAL_TENSOR_DISABLE=1 ./build/bin/test-backend-ops perf -o MUL_MAT_ID -b MTL0 \
  -p "type_a=(q4_0|q4_K|iq2_xs),.*,n=(32|64|128|256|512),"
```

| mean rows per expert | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| change | -41.2% | -40.8% | -40.6% | -22.6% | -12.0% | -8.8% |

Median over `q4_0`, `q4_K`, and `iq2_xs`.

All 30 case medians improve. 119 of 120 paired runs are faster.

The gain is larger on this path because all four simdgroups otherwise run `simdgroup_multiply_accumulate` over the full tile regardless of `nr1`.

## End to end

`Tiel-Coder-35B-A3B` IQ3_XXS, 256 experts top-8, Apple M5, against the same master.

```sh
./build/bin/llama-bench -m <model>.gguf \
  -p 512 -n 0 -fa 1 -r 5 -ub 256,512

./build/bin/llama-batched-bench -m <model>.gguf \
  -c 16384 -b 512 -ub 256 -fa on \
  -npp 128 -ntg 32 -npl 1,8,32,64
```

| test | throughput change | runs faster |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| pp512, `-ub 256` | +5.1% | 8/8 |
| pp512, `-ub 512` | +2.9% | 8/8 |
| tg64, batch 1 | +0.00% | 3/6 |
| batched decode, `npl = 8` | -0.3% | 1/4 |
| batched decode, `npl = 32` | +3.6% | 3/4 |
| batched decode, `npl = 64` | +2.6% | 4/4 |

Positive is faster.

Batch-1 decode is unchanged, as expected, because it uses `mul_mv_id`.

The batched cases start using `mul_mm_id` at 32 tokens, which is also where the gain appears.

## Testing

```sh
./build/bin/test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT_ID -b MTL0
./build/bin/test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT    -b MTL0

GGML_METAL_TENSOR_DISABLE=1 ./build/bin/test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT_ID -b MTL0
GGML_METAL_TENSOR_DISABLE=1 ./build/bin/test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT    -b MTL0
```

On `5bda51bf`:

- `MUL_MAT_ID`: 843/843 passed, 78 not supported
- `MUL_MAT`: 1265/1265 passed, 417 not supported

Both pass with tensor ops enabled and disabled.

This PR adds 33 test cases across `q4_K`, `iq2_xs`, and `f16`.

Thirty use `n_used == n_mats == 4`, so every token routes to every expert and each expert receives exactly `n` rows.

The new `mul_mm_id` cases cover the split boundary and tail sizes directly:

| n | final tile |
| ---: | ---: |
| 32 | 32 rows |
| 33 | 1 row |
| 47 | 15 rows |
| 48 | 16 rows |
| 49 | 17 rows |

The 16- and 17-row cases cover the point where the upper half starts running again.

`n = 1, 15, 16, 17, 31` cover the `mul_mv_id` path. Three additional cases use eight experts with one selected to cover empty experts.

`test_mul_mat_id` also redraws expert IDs between timed perf iterations through `reinit_perf_iter`, so perf runs do not repeatedly use the same routing assignment.

## Related

#25377, #27370 and #26223 touch nearby code. #26223 changes the same B-tile staging code, so whichever lands second will need a small merge.

items.title: metal : single-source fusion table + fusion debug rework

labels.name: devops
labels.description: improvements to build systems and github actions

labels.name: ggml
labels.description: changes relating to the ggml tensor library for machine learning

items.body:
## Overview

Rework the Metal op fusion into a single source of truth: a fixed pattern table (`ggml_metal_fusions`) consumed by both the graph optimizer (packing) and the op encoders (compute), so the two phases can never disagree about which nodes fuse. Also add a fused `gated_delta_net + cpy` pattern that writes recurrent state snapshots directly into the KV cache, eliding the trailing cpy.

## Fusion regression test

Add a new test tool `test-fusion` that validates the fusion logic against a committed per-device CSV baseline. It runs every dummy model generated by `test-llama-archs` on a single device with fusion enabled and disabled, and reports the per-fusion-type counters plus the NMSE between the fused/unfused and device/CPU logits.

- The counters are gathered through an ad-hoc `get_proc_address` API. `ggml_backend_fusion_get` resolves the device fusion context once and returns an opaque `ggml_backend_fusion_t` handle; the stats functions (`ggml_backend_fusion_stats_init/reset/get/set_enabled`) operate on that handle instead of the backend device.
- The device owns a shared fusion context that every new backend context registers with, forcing single-threaded encoding while stats are collected, so the counters are race-free and accumulate across contexts.
- A fusion pattern that silently stops matching (or fires when it should not) is caught as a regression by comparing the counters against the committed `tests/fusion/MTL.csv` baseline.
- The unfused run doubles as a control: its counters must be all-zero.
- Prefill and decode usually produce the same per-graph count for the deterministic table, so the baseline stores a single `any` row per label (150 rows for Metal) instead of separate rows per mode.
- Both the count and the NMSE checks are hard gates. Two archs needed fixes to pass: plamo2 (graph fix) and qwen3tts (the codec-head `-inf` padding made the NMSE NaN; the dummy model now uses the exact codec-head vocab so the padding is not generated).
- The dummy models are generated in a separate CI step (`test_llama_archs_models`). The test itself runs gated on `GG_BUILD_METAL` atm, but can be extended in the future to other backends.

## Additional information

- `ggml_metal_fusion` gains an `unsafe` flag for fusions that are **not** elision chains (e.g. gdn + cache cpy). The generic chain/shape and `ggml_can_fuse_subgraph_ext` checks assume a linear element-wise chain with shape-preserving ops and intermediates consumed only within the pattern; the gdn+cpy fusion violates all three (the cpy reads a view of the gdn, shapes differ, and the gdn output feeds other consumers). For `unsafe` patterns those generic checks are skipped and the pattern-specific check callback becomes the sole validator, so it must re-establish the safety guarantees itself (op sequence, no graph output, exact snapshot-tail offset, cache layout, allocation).
- Packing (`ggml_metal_fuse_max`) now matches on the same view-transparent node sequence the compute phase uses, so fused groups (including intermediate views) stay adjacent through the reorder.
- The gated_delta_net kernel writes snapshots straight into the cache buffer (`nb_out` slot stride), so the trailing cpy is elided. (from https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25788)
- Verified on Metal: full `test-backend-ops` MTL0 suite passes (0 failures), including the new `GATED_DELTA_NET_CACHE_FUSION` tests; `test-fusion --check` passes (150 rows); Qwen3.5-0.8B Q8_0 shows no regression (~+5% tg from the fusion).

items.body:
## Overview

This improves `iq3_xxs` mul-mv thread utilization when `nb32 < 32` and `nb32` divides 32.

Each thread currently takes one 32-element chunk based on its thread ID. At `ne00 = 512`, there are only 16 chunks (`nb32 = 16`), so threads 16 through 31 have nothing to process. The patch assigns two threads to each chunk, with each thread covering half of the `nr0` output rows. When `nb32 >= 32`, or `nb32` does not divide 32, the existing mapping is unchanged.

The PR also changes `N_R0_IQ3_XXS` from 4 to 8, so each simdgroup handles up to eight rows. This was tuned separately while testing; see the benchmark results below. I can revert it if this feels too specific.

Tested on my 14inch MacBook Pro M5 24 GB , using Tiel-Coder-35B-A3B IQ3_XXS.

On a fixed replay of the same coding-agent workload, the `b10488` development tree improved from 24.66 to 22.59 s/rep (−8.4% wall), with decode increasing from 65.6 to 73.9 tok/s and perplexity unchanged at 3.3969.

## Additional information

`test-backend-ops` comparisons against the CPU backend pass for `MUL_MAT_ID` and `MUL_MAT`, including `k = 256`, the deepest split, and `k = 768`, the fallback path.

| 4  | 263.91      | 218.67              | 170.11                       | −35.5%          |

The measured case is `ne00 = 512` (`nb32 = 16`). Other `iq3_xxs` matrices with `nb32 < 32`, where `nb32` divides 32, take the same row-split path.

## Summary
This PR turns the convolution into a matrix multiply for better performance. 
- Each output channel becomes a row of the weight matrix, and each output pixel becomes a column made of the input values under the kernel window. Each threadgroup gathers the values it needs straight into threadgroup memory and multiplies them with the simdgroup matrix instructions, the same way kernel_mul_mm works.
- Inputs are staged as f16 and accumulated in f32, so the numerics match what mul_mm already does for f32 matmuls.
- A threadgroup computes a 64x32 tile of the output (channels x pixels), or 32x64 when there are 32 or fewer output channels. The old kernel stays as the fallback for GPUs without simdgroup matrix support.

## Overview

The CPU FWHT accepts F32 input only. This change adds F16 input.

`ggml_compute_forward_fwht` now takes the source type as a template parameter. The CPU path accepts F16 input and F32 input. The CPU MUL_MAT reference converts an F16 `src1` to F32 when the caller sets `GGML_HINT_SRC0_IS_HADAMARD`.

The change touches `ggml-cpu` only. It is 3 files.

## Additional information

This is the first change of a small series. The later changes add F16 kernels to the backends, and add the 1024 and 2048 widths. This change is first because it sets the reference behaviour.

There are no test cases here. No backend has an F16 FWHT kernel yet, so a test would have no backend to compare the CPU result against. The test cases come with the first backend change.

`test-backend-ops` already has a width-1024 case with the comment `too big (N>512)`. A later change covers that width.

I did not build the CUDA, Metal, or Vulkan backends. This change does not touch them.

items.body:
## Overview

Adds the TQ1_0 ternary type (1.6875 bpw, base-3 packing — format by @compilade, thanks for TQ1_0/TQ2_0!) to the Vulkan backend. This was one of the last "TODO: implement for all backends" holes for this type, so consider it closed on Vulkan now.

What's in here:
- `block_tq1_0` struct + dequant functions, scalar and coopmat2 both
- mul_mm support in `mul_mm_funcs.glsl`
- Two new shaders: `mul_mat_vec_tq1_0.comp`, `dequant_tq1_0.comp`
- Pipeline creation + op-support wiring in `ggml-vulkan.cpp`
- Enabled TQ1_0 in test-backend-ops type lists, and added some MUL_MAT_ID cases at real MoE decode shapes (n=1, 28/128/512 experts, k=2048/4096)

Why I bothered adding those specific shapes: turns out the mat-vec shaders get `a_offset` already in block units from `get_offsets()`. My first draft divided by QUANT_K again on top of that — which is fine at offset 0 (nothing to divide, basically), but during actual mul_mat_id decode it just quietly grabs the wrong expert. No crash, no error, just wrong output. The normal test matrix never has n<16 or offset≠0 so it sailed right past. Adding these shapes would've caught it in five seconds instead of me staring at garbled output for an hour wondering what I broke. Figured it's worth keeping in the suite for whoever ports the next quant type too.

## Additional information

Ran this on my AMD Radeon 8060S (RDNA3.5 / gfx1151):

```
test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT      → tq1_0 11/11 OK
test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT_ID   → tq1_0 6/6 OK
test-backend-ops test -o GET_ROWS    → tq1_0 4/4 OK
```

Also did a real run: 397B MoE, all 512 experts in TQ1_0, attention kept in Q8_0, fully resident in 96 GiB UMA on one APU. Got 10+ t/s decode, wiki PPL 5.8 — better than the best sub-2-bit quant currently out there for the same model (7.0 PPL).

Running `llama-cli` with `OBJC_DEBUG_MISSING_POOLS=YES` on Mac shows various memory leaks in the Metal init path that look like this:
